news.Title: Earnings live updates: Airbnb stock jumps as Wall Street cheers 'growth mode,' upbeat outlook
news.Content:
The third quarter earnings season is over halfway done, and the reports continue to pour in. This week brought another shot of major earnings courtesy of Apple ( AAPL ), Palantir ( PLTR ), and AMD ( AMD ).

In addition to those tech heavyweights, investors are watching the results out of Roku ( ROKU ), Arm Holdings ( ARM ), McDonald's ( MCD ), QUALCOMM ( QCOM ), Novo Nordisk ( NVO ), Uber Technologies ( UBER ), Toyota Motor Corporation ( TM ), ConocoPhillips ( COP ), and Moderna ( MRNA ).

S&P 500 corporations continue to demonstrate robust earnings growth. According to FactSet data , approximately 60% of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings, with an overall earnings growth rate of 30.2%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25% for the index.

LIVE 13 updates

Featured

Thu, November 5, 2026 at 10:06 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Airbnb 'back in growth mode,' CEO says after strong quarter. Stock jumps after hours.

Airbnb ( ABNB ) stock jumped 11% after hours after the peer-to-peer home rental company touted strong growth across its business and raised its full-year outlook amid healthy global travel demand.

"Airbnb is back in growth mode," CEO Brian Chesky said in a release to investors. "It's rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that's exactly what we're doing. In Q3, we delivered our fastest revenue growth in more than three years, with acceleration across our business, including our most established markets."

In the third quarter, Airbnb reported earnings per share of $3.16, surpassing Wall Street analyst estimates of $2.85 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data. Revenue grew 19% to $4.87 billion, also beating estimates of $4.74 billion.

"In North America, nights booked grew at their fastest pace in four years," the company said. "We're also seeing more guests return to Airbnb, and more people try it for the first time."

The strength of the company's quarter led it to raise its guidance for the remainder of the year.

In the fourth quarter, Airbnb expects revenue to grow 16%-19% to a range of $3.22 billion to $3.28 billion, exceeding the Street's midpoint estimate of $3.16 billion.

For the full year, Airbnb forecasts revenue growth in the high teens and adjusted EBITDA margins to increase to approximately 36%.

Thu, November 5, 2026 at 10:09 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Atlassian tumbles 16% on weaker subscription growth outlook

Investing.com reports:

Atlassian Corporation shares plunged 16% despite the company reporting first-quarter results that topped analyst expectations, as its subscription growth outlook disappointed investors.

The collaboration software provider reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.65, beating analyst estimates of $1.43 by $0.22. Revenue rose 24% year-over-year to $1.77 billion from $1.43 billion a year earlier, surpassing the consensus estimate of $1.71 billion. Adjusted operating margin also came in ahead of expectations at 32%, compared with the estimated 28.6%.

However, investors focused on signs of slowing subscription growth. Atlassian forecast subscription annual recurring revenue (ARR) growth of approximately 18.5% year-over-year for fiscal 2027, down from the 23% growth reported in the first quarter.

Thu, November 5, 2026 at 9:52 PM UTC Brooke DiPalma

Bob's Furniture stock rises after better-than-expected results: 'Value is always in vogue'

Bob's Furniture ( BOBS ) reported better-than-expected third quarter results. Revenue came in at $680 million, higher than the $666 million estimates, per Bloomberg consensus data. Adjusted earnings per share also beat estimates by $0.02, coming in at $0.28.

The results were largely driven by customers leaning into higher-cost furniture, with CEO Bill Barton telling Yahoo Finance, "Value is always in vogue."

"The industry continues to struggle, although we think ... the furniture industry stabilized a bit in the third quarter. We're not really calling for a turn yet, ... [but] the trend that we saw in the spring of our customers trading up into the premium price tiers continued in the third quarter. So we saw that average order value going up, and that's really what carried a lot of the comp growth for the third quarter," Barton said.

The company reaffirmed its 2026 guidance, with expectations for same-store sales to grow in the range of 1.5% to 2.5%, but it didn't update its guidance, with Barton calling it a "very dynamic backdrop."

Wed, November 4, 2026 at 9:23 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Qualcomm tops Q4 estimates, but Q1 earnings outlook falls short

Yahoo Finance's Dan Howley reports:

Qualcomm ( QCOM ) reported fourth quarter earnings after the bell Wednesday, topping expectations on the top and bottom lines and providing a better-than-anticipated Q1 revenue outlook.

But a lower-than-expected midpoint for its earnings per share (EPS) forecast send shares lower following the report.

For Q4, Qualcomm reported adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.17 on revenue of $10.32 billion. Analysts were projecting EPS of $2.16 and revenue of $10.12 billion.

The company saw EPS of $3.00 and revenue of $11.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Qualcomm also offered Q1 revenue guidance of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion, with the midpoint ahead of Wall Street's $10.6 billion outlook.

EPS, though, is set to come in between $2.15 and $2.35 with a midpoint of $2.25. Analysts were looking for $2.32

Wed, November 4, 2026 at 9:18 PM UTC Brooke DiPalma

Cava results fall just shy of estimates due to impact of cyclospora outbreak. Company raises outlook.

Mediterranean fast-casual chain Cava ( CAVA ) posted earnings and revenue that fell short of Wall Street's expectations as the company saw strength to end the quarter, following industry pressure.

Cava revenue came in at $353.7 million, below the $358.7 million the Street expected, per Bloomberg estimates. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.11, one penny lower than forecasts. Same-store sales grew by 3.1%, a touch lower than the 3.3% the Street hoped for.

"We saw obviously broader concerns around fresh produce consumption early in the quarter that certainly impacted trend, we saw that bounce back as we worked through the quarter and then toward the end of the quarter," CEO Brett Schulman told Yahoo Finance.

Schulman added, "Post Labor Day, we did see a bit of choppiness around the re-emergence of high gas prices as they spiked, but then saw that abate, things firm up and strengthen as we exited the quarter and have seen that carryover into Q4."

He said that gave the company confidence to raise its outlook for the full fiscal year. It now expects same-store sales to increase between 6% and 7%, up from the previously expected range of 4.5% to 6.5%. The updated forecast is in line with the Street's 6.7% expectation.

The company plans to open 76 to 78 restaurants this year, but the company noted that pre-opening costs did get more expensive, driven by pre-opening labor costs. Its new restaurant design is also resonating with customers, who are seeing an increase in in-restaurant dining, especially at dinner. Schulman said that's not at the expense of digital orders, which account for 38.5% of revenue.

Tue, November 3, 2026 at 9:33 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

AMD beats Q3 estimates as data center revenue climbs 97%

AMD ( AMD ) reported its third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday, beating expectations on the top and bottom lines, as the company's data center revenue grew 97%.

AMD stock climbed more than 4% following the news.

"Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and 'Venice' production," CEO Lisa Su said in a statement.

"With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years."

For the quarter, AMD saw earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 on revenue of $13.38 billion. Analysts were projecting EPS of $1.97 on revenue of $13.08 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.

The company saw EPS and revenue of $1.20 and $9.2 billion, respectively, in the same period last year.

Tue, November 3, 2026 at 9:32 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Duolingo stock jumps as daily users surge, company raises guidance

Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock jumped 10% after the company reported that its daily active users (DAUs) rose 29% year over year to 64.9 million. Paid subscribers for the language learning platform grew 14% annually to 13.1 million.

But the company is eyeing stronger user growth as it targets a goal of 1 billion users. Duolingo said its operating expenses increased 24% year over year. Those expenses included $11.4 million that the company set aside for a company-wide performance bonus for employees if it achieves DAU growth of 25% or greater in Q4.

Here's what Duolingo reported in Q3, versus estiamtes compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:

Revenue: $309 million, up 12% year over year, versus estimates of $303 million

Earnings per share: $0.58, versus estimates of $0.56

Guidance: Raised across all key financial metrics. Revenue is expected at $1.22 billion, ahead of the Street's forecast of $1.20 billion

"We expect to finish 2026 at the high end of both the 10% to 12% bookings growth and 15% to 18% revenue growth targets we set at the start of the year. We expect full-year Adjusted EBITDA of $323 million, or a 26.5% margin, up $3 million from our previous guidance, and $21 million above the midpoint of our original 2026 guidance provided in February," the company stated.

Tue, November 3, 2026 at 9:19 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Super Micro tops Q1 estimates, offers strong Q2 outlook

Yahoo Finance's Daniel Howley reports:

Data center infrastructure company Super Micro ( SMCI ) reported its fiscal first quarter earnings after the bell on Tuesday, beating Wall Street's expectations on the top and bottom lines and providing a better-than-anticipated outlook for Q2.

The company said it anticipates Q2 sales of between $19.5 billion and $21.5 billion. Analysts were calling for $16.35 billion.

Super Micro stock rose more than 5% immediately following the news.

"Supermicro's transformation into a Total AI and IT Datacenter Solution provider continues to accelerate, delivering record revenue of $19.9 billion for the first quarter fiscal 2027," CEO Charles Liang said in a statement.

"DCBBS is driving significant value for our customers—from gigawatt-scale datacenters down to single-container PODs—which, including our expanding software, proactive service, and networking solutions, is enhancing profitability and long-term shareholder value. Through key enterprise partnerships and expanding global production capacity, we are making AI infrastructure faster to deploy, superior up-time and more cost-effective for our customer base."

Tue, November 3, 2026 at 5:20 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Pfizer focuses on GLP-1, oncology drug development as COVID product sales decline

Pfizer ( PFE ) stock fell slightly on Tuesday despite reporting an earnings beat and upbeat guidance. The pharmaceutical company said it saw operational revenue growth contributions from several treatments, including Eliquis, Paxlovid, the Vyndaqel family, Nurtec, and Lorbrena, during the quarter, though its COVID-19 products declined.

In the earnings call, Pfizer said it expects to spend $10.8 billion-$11.8 billion on research and development this year, particularly on developing its oncology and obesity pipeline. Pfizer is working on berobenatide, a GLP-1 injectable administered only once a month rather than weekly, as well as several cancer drugs.

"Pfizer had another strong quarter with commercial momentum and disciplined execution while advancing our strategy for creating long-term shareholder value," CEO Albert Bourla said in a release. "Our obesity program continued to advance and recent milestones in oncology, immunology and vaccines further demonstrate the potential of our pipeline."

In the third quarter, Pfizer reported revenue was little changed year over year at $16.6 billion, ahead of analyst estimates of $15.9 billion, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Earnings per share came in at $0.56, beating Wall Street's estimates of $0.48 per share.

Pfizer lifted its full-year revenue guidance to a range of $62 billion to $64 billion, up from $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion previously. The company also raised and narrowed its 2026 earnings per share guidance to $2.95 to $3.05.

Tue, November 3, 2026 at 4:37 PM UTC Ines Ferré

Shopify stock tanks as Q3 revenue, total order value miss Wall Street estimates

Shopify ( SHOP ) stock plunged 7% on Tuesday after reporting third quarter results that missed the mark on several key metrics.

The cloud-based e-commerce platform's Q3 revenue of $3.74 billion came in just shy of consensus estimates of $3.75 billion for the first time since 2022, according to Bloomberg data. Subscription revenue for the quarter of $836 million also missed Wall Street expectations of $850.2 million, raising concerns about growth in its main recurring-revenue business.

Gross merchandise volume, or the total dollar value of orders sold through Shopify's platform, was $119.15 billion, also falling short of estimates of $120.08 billion.

Shopify's adjusted earnings per share of $0.49 topped estimates of $0.48.

Mon, November 2, 2026 at 9:39 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Apple tops Q4 estimates on strong iPhone sales, but misses on China revenue

Apple ( AAPL ) stock is declining in extended trading after beating on earnings but missing on China revenue.

Yahoo Finance's Dan Howley reports on the quarter:

Apple reported its fourth quarter earnings after the bell on Monday, beating expectations on the top and bottom lines on strong iPhone sales.

This is Apple's first earnings call with new CEO John Ternus , who took over the role from Tim Cook on Sept. 1.

For the quarter, Apple reported earnings per share (EPS) of $2.10 on revenue of $114.48 billion. Wall Street was looking for EPS of $2 on revenue of $113.46 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates.

The company saw EPS of $1.85 and revenue of $102.46 billion in the same period last year.

Read live updates and analysis from the quarter and earnings call >

Mon, November 2, 2026 at 9:24 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Roku sales grow 24% year over year ahead of Fox acquisition

Roku ( ROKU ) reported a substantial earnings beat on Monday, driven by its ninth straight quarter of double-digit advertising growth.

Here's what Roku reported, compared to Wall Street analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:

Revenue : up 24% year over year to $1.5 billion, versus estimates of $1.41 billion.

Advertising revenue grew 23% YoY to $727 million.

Subscriptions revenue grew 23% YoY to $581 million.

Earnings per share: $1.20, versus estimates of $0.55.

Guidance: None given.

Roku stock was little changed following the report.

In June, Roku entered an agreement to be acquired by Fox ( FOX ). The company said that, in light of its pending takeover, it would not host an earnings call or provide a forecast.

"Our third quarter demonstrated that we succeed when our partners succeed, whether it is a streaming service gaining subscribers through Premium Subscriptions, a content company monetizing its library on The Roku Channel, an advertiser buying through a third-party DSP, or a TV brand choosing the Roku TV OS," CEO Anthony Wood wrote in a press release.

Mon, November 2, 2026 at 9:11 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell

Palantir raises full-year revenue outlook as US commercial sales accelerate

Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferré reports:

Palantir ( PLTR ) beat Wall Street estimates on its third quarter revenue and profit on Monday and raised its full-year revenue outlook as the data software company's US commercial business surpassed its US government sales for the first time ever.

Palantir reported Q3 revenue of $2.313 billion, a 96% increase from the previous year. Wall Street had expected revenue of $2.17 billion, according to Bloomberg data.

Palantir now sees full-year revenue between $8.530 billion and $8.534 billion, topping analyst estimates of $8.2 billion. The company also raised its US commercial sales target to more than $3.559 billion. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.44 also beat consensus estimates of $0.40.

news.Title: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
news.Content:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.

Thursday did a lot of the damage . Nvidia closed down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a single session and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. It was the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.

Nvidia has plenty of company.

AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) suffered steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) fell more than 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) had its worst day since March 2020 and is now more than a third below its June record. Sandisk ( SNDK ) dropped 22%.

Nvidia itself is now about 24% below its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .

The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.

Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.

The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.

That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.

For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.

"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

news.Title: Qualcomm, Micron, Sandisk, and AMD stocks sink, leading chip sector lower
news.Content:
Chip stocks plummeted on Thursday, extending declines from the prior session, with Qualcomm ( QCOM ), Micron Technology ( MU ), Sandisk ( SDNK ), and AMD ( AMD ) falling by double-digit percentages. Despite a broader market rally on Wednesday following Democrats' midterm election victory, semiconductor stocks moved lower amid the threat that stricter regulation could slow data center construction.

Semiconductor stocks, which drove the AI trade higher this year, have been volatile since the summer. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell by 12%, trimming the index's year-to-date gains to roughly 25%.

The declines were led by Qualcomm, which issued an underwhelming profit forecast , signaling that higher-cost components are weighing on the smartphone processor maker.

Shares of Arm Holdings ( ARM ) also fell 13% after the chip designer issued revenue guidance that, while slightly above consensus, failed to impress investors who priced in a higher range amid the AI boom.

Micron Technology stock also declined after the memory chipmaker paused plans for a Taiwanese plant due to labor disputes. Sandisk slid 22%, extending declines from 7% in the prior session.

SK Hynix ( SKHY ) also declined after shares of the South Korean memory maker tumbled overseas, alongside Samsung Electronics ( 005930.K S ).

At the same time, shares of US chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) declined about 10%, while AMD plunged 17%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) also extended declines from the prior session.

news.Title: Arm Holdings (ARM) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Vice President of Investor Relations - Ian Thornton

Chief Executive Officer - Rene Haas

Chief Financial Officer - Jason Child

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Ian Thornton, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Ian Thornton: Thank you very much, and welcome to our second quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call. On the call are Rene Haas, Arm's Chief Executive Officer, and Jason Child, Arm's Chief Financial Officer. Today's call contains forward-looking information about the company and its financial results. While these statements represent our best current judgment, our business is subjected to many risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Important risk factors that may affect our business and future financial results are described in our annual report on Form 20-F filed with the SEC. Arm assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. We will also refer to non-GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliations of these non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in our shareholder letter, as can the discussion of certain projected non-GAAP financial measures that we're not able to reconcile without unreasonable effort and supplemental financial information. Our earnings materials are available at investors.arm.com. With that, I'll turn the call over to Rene.

Rene Haas: Thank you, Ian, and good afternoon, everyone. Arm delivered a record second quarter. Revenue reached $1.44 billion, up 27% year-over-year, marking our fifth straight quarter of growth above 20%. License and other revenue grew 50% to $773 million, driven by our partners increasing their investment in the Arm Compute Platform. This strong licensing momentum is an important leading indicator of future royalties, which we expect to accelerate as these new designs enter production. Second quarter royalty revenue grew 8% to $670 million, with data center royalties doubling year-over-year. Non-GAAP earnings per share increased 33% to $0.52, while we continue to increase our investment in R&D.

AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute across the cloud, devices, and autonomous systems, with Arm being the compute platform of choice. Today, our business is now driven by two rapidly growing areas: the IP business, where partners are increasing investment in the Arm Compute Platform and deploying record numbers of Arm-based chips, and our new silicon business, where demand for the Arm AGI CPU is extremely strong. Both leverage the same Arm Compute Platform and software ecosystem. We are seeing these two growth vectors play out clearly in the data center, where our partners are expanding their deployment of Arm-based infrastructure alongside strong demand for Arm-designed silicon.

Story Continues

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, OCI, is a key example of how these two businesses reinforce one another. Today, OCI offers NVIDIA Vera CPUs built on Arm, and in addition, plans to offer Arm AGI CPU instances in 2027. Since launching the Arm AGI CPU in March, customer demand has continued to strengthen. We have secured purchase orders from multiple customers extending through calendar 2027, and first commercial deliveries remain on track for fiscal Q4 2027. Our confidence in achieving up to $2 billion of revenue in Arm AGI CPU across fiscal 2027 and 2028 has increased over the last 90 days, supported by additional supply and customer mix. We remain focused on expanding capacity to meet growing customer demand.

Power availability makes performance and efficiency even more important. Morgan Stanley projects a 38 GW global data center power shortfall through 2028. Arm is helping customers address this constraint by delivering more useful compute from the power already available. At OCP, independent testing by Signal65 showed the Arm AGI CPU delivering approximately twice the performance per rack versus the AMD EPYC 9755. This type of improvement could reduce the projected global power shortfall by half. Our data center royalties doubled year-over-year, and Arm-based server market share at the top hyperscalers has more than tripled from 15% in calendar 2024 to more than 50% in calendar 2025.

Based upon expected ramps across Google Axion, AWS Graviton, Microsoft Cobalt, and NVIDIA platforms, we now expect that share to exceed 60% by the end of calendar 2026. Beyond the data center, Arm's role in edge AI increases as AI agents become more capable and persistent. Arm-based PCs have now reached 20% of global shipments. Google recently announced Googlebook, a new category of AI-native laptops built for Gemini intelligence, with Arm serving as the primary compute platform for many models. NVIDIA's RTX Spark systems, which are now available, further expand Arm into local AI, content creation, and gaming. In smartphones, Arm recently announced CSS for Mobile 2, which improves performance of agentic AI workloads by up to 70% through SME2.

Our first AI-native Mali GPU delivers up to four times the frame rate at the same sustained power. These capabilities allow more AI and richer experiences to run directly on the device without compromising battery life. Arm is the platform of choice for physical AI. Royalty revenue grew 50% year-over-year, driven by advanced driver assistance and in-vehicle infotainment. We also launched Arm Total Design for Physical AI, bringing together more than 80 companies to accelerate the development and deployment of complete physical AI systems. For the first time, our partners reported more than 10 billion Arm-based chips shipped in a single quarter, an increase of 1.5 billion year-on-year, supported by a software ecosystem of more than 30 million developers.

Demand for Arm technology has never been stronger, as AI is driving more complex designs and greater demand for power-efficient compute. Our IP business generates licensing revenue as those designs begin and royalties as they enter production. Arm AGI CPU adds a new direct silicon business built on the same compute platform and software ecosystem. That gives Arm two powerful growth engines, which we expect to accelerate revenue at a faster pace in the future. With that, I will turn it over to Jason.

Jason Child: Thank you, Rene. We delivered another strong quarter, with total revenue growing 27% year-on-year to $1.44 billion. This was a record for our second quarter and our second-highest quarterly revenue ever, reflecting continued strength in our business. License and other revenue was $773 million, up 50% year-on-year, also a record for the second quarter and our second-highest quarter ever. License revenue was around $100 million higher than we had anticipated due to an acceleration of interest from customers wanting to sign long-term commitments to access Arm technology. During the quarter, we signed three new Arm Total Access agreements, bringing the total number of active ATA subscriptions to more than 60.

This included one of our major customers signing their first ATA license. We also signed four additional compute subsystem licenses, two for data center chips and two for smartphones. For established customers, these agreements broaden and deepen access to our future technology roadmap and provide an important foundation for Arm's future royalty growth. In addition, we are seeing ATA and CSS as a way for newer customers who have previously made only limited use of Arm technology to accelerate their adoption, with several signing ATA or CSS licenses during the quarter. Of the $773 million in license revenue, our agreement with SoftBank for technology licensing and design services contributed $209 million, up 17% year-on-year.

We expect the quarterly run rate for the rest of the year to remain around this level. Annualized contract value grew 12% year-on-year. As we have discussed before, license revenue can vary significantly from quarter to quarter based on the timing and accounting treatment of large agreements, so ACV remains a useful measure of the underlying licensing trend. Turning now to royalty. Royalty revenue was $670 million, up 8% year-on-year, also our highest-ever figure for Q2. Cloud AI remained the largest growth driver. Once again, data center royalty doubled year-on-year as Arm-based CPUs ramp across AI infrastructure and general-purpose cloud workloads. Physical AI royalty revenue grew 50% year-on-year, driven by increasing adoption of Arm technology in automotive and robotics.

In edge AI, royalty revenue was roughly flat year-on-year. Higher memory prices continue to pressure smartphone unit sales, particularly in the mid and lower-tier segments. That headwind was offset by the benefit we continue to see from higher royalty rates as our latest Armv9 and CSS technologies are adopted. As smartphone market conditions normalize, we expect edge AI royalty revenue to reaccelerate. As Rene discussed, customer demand for the Arm AGI CPU remains very strong. Last quarter, we said that we had increased confidence in achieving more than $1 billion across fiscal year 2027 and 2028.

In the past 90 days, we have signed purchase orders from multiple customers and signed supply agreements with companies in our supply chain, giving us increased confidence in achieving up to $2 billion across fiscal 2027 and 2028. We will provide another update at our Q3 results, which is when we will have better visibility. Turning to operating expenses and profits. Non-GAAP operating expense was $774 million, up 19% year-on-year, as we continued to expand our engineering capacity and invest in next-generation platforms, compute subsystems, and our Arm AGI CPU product family. Non-GAAP operating income was $638 million, up 37% year-on-year. Non-GAAP operating margin was 44.2%, up 300 basis points from a year ago, as revenue outpaced operating expense growth.

Non-GAAP EPS was $0.52, up 33% year-on-year. Importantly, even at these elevated levels of investment, we generate free cash flow of $1.1 billion over the trailing 12 months, giving us the flexibility to continue to invest for long-term growth. Turning now to guidance. For Q3, we expect revenue of $1.54 billion, $±50 million. At the midpoint, this represents growth of approximately 24% year-on-year. We expect continued strong growth in license and other revenue, up a little over 50% year-on-year, supported by strong customer demand and our visibility into the licensing pipeline.

In royalties, we expect continued strength in cloud AI and physical AI, offset by ongoing pressure in edge AI from weaker smartphone demand, and we have a tough year-on-year comp. As a result, we expect royalty revenue to grow low teens sequentially and low single digits year-on-year. We expect non-GAAP operating expenses of approximately $825 million and non-GAAP EPS of $0.56, $±0.04. Looking further ahead, we continue to see strong customer demand across our business. Combined with the expansion of our technology portfolio and deepening strategic customer relationships, this gives us confidence in our long-term growth outlook. With that, I will turn the call back to the operator for Q&A.

Operator: Thank you. To ask a question, you will need to press star one and one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one and one again. We will now go to the first question. One moment, please. Your first question today comes from the line of Gary Mobley from StoneX Group. Please go ahead.

Gary Mobley: Good afternoon, everybody. Thanks for taking my question. I think on the top of the mind for everybody is Arm AGI CPU, and you are obviously signaling something closer to $2 billion in revenue over the five-quarter period up to the end of fiscal year 2028. I am wondering what is driving your confidence into that with respect to securing more supply with your different partners. I would assume most of the revenue initially goes to supporting Meta, but maybe if you can talk about whether or not you have signed and committed contractually with additional customers.

Rene Haas: Yeah. Thanks, Gary. I will take that question, and Jason can add if I have missed anything. Each one of the quarters, as we talk about the ramp of the product, we have been careful to make sure that we manage the expectations of supply and demand. I think there is no secret that, in general, demand is incredibly strong for the Arm AGI CPU, really driven by everything we see with agentic workloads and the CPU being central to that. Demand is stronger today than we talked about when we did the Arm Everywhere event in March, and subsequently, demand from multiple customers, Meta being the chief customer, has also been beyond what we have expected.

That being said, we have been working very hard over the last few quarters on securing what is necessary in the supply chain to address that demand. There are multiple components to it. There is wafer supply, there are substrates, there are testers, there is memory, et cetera. We have wanted to be confident when we signal our ability to achieve this extra demand with supply in the ongoing quarters. So at Arm Everywhere Day, we talked about visibilities of $1 billion, and quickly, we have seen that to about a $2 billion number.

I can tell you today that the confidence is the strongest it has been to date, and it is definitely stronger than it was 90 days ago in terms of securing that supply. As I said, it is across all of those independent areas. We did not start working on it yesterday or the previous quarter. We have been working on it actually for the last number of quarters. We have got great partners who are supporting us here, and as you mentioned, Meta is a chief customer, but there will be multiple customers beyond Meta. Jason, I do not know if there is anything that you want to add. If not, thanks, Gary, for the question.

Operator: Thank you.

Gary Mobley: If I could ask.

Operator: Please continue, Gary.

Gary Mobley: My apologies. I was just hoping to ask a follow-up question briefly. You have given us enough information in the shareholder letter to calculate your royalty rate per unit on a year-over-year basis, and it looks like it is trending up at least mid-single-digit percent. I am wondering if that is just sort of an anomaly with respect to mix or if that should be how we view the royalty rate per unit growth over the long term.

Jason Child: Yeah. I mean, it's mixed, but it's also, I think we said, what, 10 billion chips shipped in the quarter. It's going to bounce around based on any particular quarter. I would say, certainly, mobile on average is probably a little lower than certainly server and physical AI, given the size and value of the chips. That probably had some impact. I do not know that I would take the overall average across 10 billion chips and use that as the best way to forecast going forward.

I do think if you break it out by the three different business units, as we said, pretty flattish growth in the mobile business, very strong double-digit growth in server, where we are also seeing increasing core counts and more CSS revenue flowing through this quarter, but we are going to continue seeing that going forward. That is why we have high confidence that we are going to have triple-digit growth for the next few years. Then on physical AI, that one is also, we said, growing 50% year-on-year. That is also going to, I would say, be a bit of a tailwind to overall royalty rates and overall royalty growth.

Again, I would probably break it into those three categories, as opposed to just looking at it all combined together.

Rene Haas: Yeah. Maybe, Gary, just a finer point on the data center growth. I think there is two vectors independent of the Arm AGI CPU on the royalty. One is Arm taking market share, which I mentioned before. Now we think it is going to be 60% by the end of the year. That market share gain is driven both in terms of units going up, agentic AI driving increased design starts for Graviton, Cobalt, Axion, et cetera. In addition, we are seeing a transition away from x86 to Arm for the head node CPU that connect to accelerators. We already know about Vera Rubin, but Google has already announced the conversion of x86 to Axion, connecting to TPU version 8.

To Jason's point, this is why we have a high degree of confidence on data center royalties growing triple digits over the next number of years.

Gary Mobley: Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please press star, one, and one on your telephone. In the interest of time, please limit yourself to one question only and rejoin the queue for any follow-ups. We will now go to our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Sebastien Naji from William Blair. Please go ahead.

Sebastien Naji: Good afternoon, and thanks for taking the question. I want to ask about how Arm wins versus x86 in the AI data center. At OCP, you introduced agentic AI benchmarks that showed your Arm AGI CPU can deliver twice the performance per rack versus a competing x86 solution. Last night on its earnings call, AMD said that its Venice CPU offers the best performance per watt. Maybe, Rene, could you talk about where you see the most meaningful opportunity for the Arm CPU to win in the data center versus x86?

Rene Haas: Yeah, sure. I'll take the question kind of from two angles. One is looking at it in the eyes of an Amazon or a Google or a Microsoft who are building custom CPUs for their own implementations and their own racks and their own systems. In those designs, particularly when an end customer is designing an SoC, the degree and flexibility that they have to innovate around their own system is extremely high. Trade-offs that they can make in terms of what goes inside the SoC for data movement versus what takes place inside a DPU, which is what takes place inside a storage.

At that level, you almost have to look at it in terms of performance per rack as versus the chip basis. At a chip level, Arm not only gives them the most efficient core on the planet, but allows them to design the most efficient SoC and subsequently the ultimate system. We've seen that just in terms of how quickly these customers have been converting designs away from standard x86 to Arm. The Arm AGI CPU benchmark that we ran, that was done through Signal65 at OCP, was looking at the previous generation to Venice, and we are very confident in those numbers, and we're very confident in terms of the choices that customers make vis-à-vis head-to-head against that design.

Venice is a great product, but we're very confident in terms of the demand we have for our product, Arm AGI CPU, and the roadmap going forward. I would say two vectors to look at it. One is just efficiency, performance per dollar, performance per watt with AGI CPU. On the custom level, there are just simply things that end customers can do that a standard product is never going to be able to touch, and that is kind of the beauty of the Arm business model.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from the line of Krish Sankar from TD Cowen. Please go ahead.

Krish Sankar: Yeah. Hi, thanks for taking my question. Rene or Jason, at OCP, you introduced your AGI CPU reference server design. I am just wondering, are you working with ODMs or server manufacturers? Are you targeting the enterprise private cloud? Along the same path on FY 2031, $15 billion AGI CPU revenues, which is the biggest factor? Is it core count increase or is it ASP increasing from the current version 1? Thank you.

Rene Haas: Yeah. No, thank you for the question. When I think about the partners that we are working with, it is Supermicro, Lenovo, and ASRock. They are building the racks for us, and then are basically standing those up for deployment at data centers such as OCI. So they are some of the partners that we build with. As far as the revenue outlook, and Jason can speak to the specifics of where we think and when we think those numbers are going to land, there is clearly going to be an acceleration of number of cores inside these SoCs.

That is largely driven by agentic workloads, and specifically the fact that each one of these agents, when you think of Muse agent that is running a specific job, typically runs as a virtual machine on one CPU core. The software is rather complex to manage that across a single core or multiple cores, if you will. If you can run that on a single core, it is a better thing. Do I see CPUs going from 128 cores to 256 cores to 500+ cores? Absolutely. You can imagine that the average selling price of the chips with more cores will be higher, certainly.

I think what we will see is probably a more rapid acceleration to that, which will help grow the top line. Jason, if any, you want to add on to that numbers-wise.

Jason Child: Yeah. No, we said back at the Arm Everywhere event last March that we had the line of sight to $1 billion for this kind of end of 2027 and FY 2028. Of course, now we are increasing our confidence to deliver $2 billion. The following year, we have not made any updates, but I think the original plan was that we were going to get to about $2 billion year after that, and then we were going to go up to about $5 billion year after that. To the extent that we are successful in delivering over $2 billion, you should expect that we will probably have some upsides after that.

That is something that we will plan on providing in terms of updated possible targets when we have the next Arm Everywhere event. We are still working on timing, but likely probably in, say, spring or first half of next year is probably when we will provide that update.

Rene Haas: Yeah, I think what we can say is when we did the Arm Everywhere day in March, the conventional wisdom was the market was a $60 billion market and was not going to be growing all that much. When we did our calculations, we felt differently, and we talked about a number that day of $100 billion by 2030. I think that number has been increased by various folks. I think Lisa may have even said $200 billion or more. I think that is about right, and maybe even could be under-calling it. Who knows?

What is obvious is that the agentic demands on AI jobs are CPU-bound, and the more agentic workloads that run, that is going to need more CPUs. I think that's what's going to end up driving these higher core count devices, which I think will be very good for us, because what's going to matter there is performance per watt at the core level, having the most efficient core on the planet, which is what we're very good at.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question today comes from the line of Mehdi Hosseini from Susquehanna. Please go ahead.

Mehdi Hosseini: Yes. Two follow-ups. Going back to the new updated Arm AGI CPU silicon revenue target of $2 billion, should we assume any revenue contribution in September or December quarter of this year, FY 2027?

Jason Child: Assume that our shipments will start in Q4. If we have something in Q3, we'll let you know. It wouldn't be a lot. We're really targeting Q4.

Mehdi Hosseini: Okay. Then just a quick follow-up. Would it be fair to say that data center mix of the royalty revenue is tracking to 1/3 or a 30%-35%, and for next fiscal year, FY 2028, it could go up towards a mid-40%?

Jason Child: I'm sorry, the—

Rene Haas: Are you asking what—

Jason Child: Mix of total royalties?

Rene Haas: Percentage of total royalties that are data center? Is that the question?

Mehdi Hosseini: Yes. Would it be fair to assume that it is tracking to like 1/3 in FY 2027, and it would step up again in 2028, moving towards 45%?

Jason Child: I mean, we look at them independently. I would assume that royalties for Edge are going to be pretty flattish this quarter, and I think we said we will start to see some recovery in Q4. But if you have that in the kind of high single digits, and then you have data center growing at double digits, and I think we said last year we were kind of approaching 20%-ish of total royalties, and then you have physical AI growing somewhere between 20%, 30%-ish range, then that is how you should build your model. I have not done the math to look at the percentage.

I do not think data center will get quite to a third, but it will sometime soon. I just do not know if it is going to get there by the end of this year.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Simon Leopold from Raymond James. Please go ahead.

Simon Leopold: Thank you very much. Appreciate you taking the question. I wanted to ask about basically the cloud and AI group of products and how you might frame the customer concentration there to help us give us a better appreciation. For example, could we guess that maybe 60% of these royalties are coming from three customers? Any kind of quantification would be helpful to understand that. Thank you.

Rene Haas: I think we can say, and Jason, chime in on this thing, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are the largest contributors, and then you've now got NVIDIA ramping up quickly. They are the four guys inside the data center that command the majority of the royalties.

Jason Child: Correct.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question today comes from the line of Harlan Sur from JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Harlan Sur: Yeah. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. With the strong success of your first-generation Arm AGI CPU, I'm sure your customers are already looking towards your next-generation platform. Can you just give us an update on second-gen AGI? I think the plan was for the team to tape out either end of this year, beginning of next year for ramping calendar 2028. Maybe just as importantly, as you continue to add more capabilities to your compute silicon portfolio, does it actually make sense to add more networking and high-performance I/O capabilities as well? More and more, we're seeing that compute and networking are very closely coupled to determine very good systems performance.

Is the team going to add more networking and capabilities to the portfolio?

Rene Haas: Yeah. Thank you, Harlan. Those are great questions. Without disclosing the precise schedule on the follow-on chip, you can think about this market goes at about an 18- to 24-month cadence in terms of production ramps. So, as we are ramping into production now on the first one, you can kind of do the math on when the second one would be available. Regarding other things that you can add to the toolbox to improve performance, whether that's around connectivity, broadly speaking, whether that's around specific I/O, and/or networking, and/or other aspects of the system, we are absolutely looking at all of that. When we think about developing these products, we're thinking about rack system performance.

The chip, the CPU is a big part of it, but how you move data in and out of the system, to your question, is as large an area as any. We have a lot of activity underway in all these areas. Nothing that we can announce here on this call, but completely cognizant of that being an area that we could have even larger differentiation.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Lee Simpson from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lee Simpson: Great. Thanks for squeezing me in. Maybe just two quick ones, if I could. Maybe first one for Jason Child. $773 million for licensing really stands out. Congratulations to everyone there. You did talk about Arm Total Access, you did talk about CSS deals, particularly smartphones, and I think data center you mentioned. But do we have any sort of architectural license agreements in there? Could we look at $770 million plus as a new level, a structural level?

Maybe for follow-on for Rene Haas, maybe in line with some of the earlier questions, it's interesting that as we look to higher ASP CPUs in the future with higher core count, could it be that we see a higher per core dollar equivalence in that pricing? In other words, playing off this capability that are associated capabilities, perhaps networking and IO as mentioned in the last question, that drives that per core dollar value up. Thanks.

Jason Child: Okay. Thanks, Lee. On your first question around license, yeah, we talk about ATA and CSS, which is the vast majority of everything that we are selling going forward. Architecture licenses are very, very few and far between. I would think of it as really being ATA and CSS. That is the bulk of most everything we are selling going forward. In terms of absolute magnitude of dollars, yeah, $773 million was a great quarter. If you, I think, kind of work out the details, I said it was going to be increasing and going up from there in this next quarter, and even in Q4, it is going to step up again.

We have not talked about next year, whether or not that is the new number every quarter. I do not know if I would say that, but I will say the pipeline has been surprisingly strong, stronger than we expected when we started the year. A little bit like the last couple years, where we have had maybe deals that were not initially They were in the pipeline, but they were not renewals. These were incremental and new deals that are kind of hard to forecast. We are in that same situation again.

What is interesting is, when we started this year, we thought it was going to be much more around royalties and that a lot of the license growth related to all the AI investments, we thought maybe we kind of had passed a lot of that. What is interesting is, it seems to be that with AI and the consistent variability, everyone is trying to address all the agentic workloads, we are seeing that the need for additional license and additional product variations and different technologies is not slowing down at all.

That is particularly exciting, as you know, any license beats, especially with ATAs and CSSs, that is very highly likely to turn into design wins and very likely to turn into even more royalties, probably 12-18 months, 24 months down the road. That is a really good setup for next year and after. We will have to, I guess, get through the next couple quarters before I can talk about next year. The pipelines do look strong. Even with the memory issues that we've seen really kind of making for some tough comps in the mobile business, which really, that does end mostly in this quarter that we're now in, Q3.

We start lapping those headwinds that really started in January, February of next year. The comps also get easier. But overall, we think it's a really good setup for the balance of this year and likely going into next year as well.

Rene Haas: Yeah. On pricing, it's a tricky one from the perspective of memory pricing has obviously increased a lot since we announced the Arm AGI CPU. Data centers are getting more and more complicated to build, whether it's through just, again, memory pricing/finding laborers, et cetera. So, while we want to be cognizant of not pushing the pricing piece too hard given all these other factors, I think it is fair to say that there's probably some pricing elasticity that we could potentially exercise on these larger chips and the chips that have higher core counts. We'll look at all of it, obviously, but I think it's fair to say that there probably is some headroom there.

Operator: Thank you. Your next question today comes from the line of Vivek Arya from Bank of America Securities. Please go ahead.

Vivek Arya: Thanks for taking my question, one for each. Jason, let's say smartphone units are down again, double-digit next year. Do you think royalties will kind of be similarly profiled to what we saw this year, or are there other dynamics at play? Rene, on the AGI platform, let's assume we believe in the technical merits. My question is, does Arm have the scale in the ecosystem to secure supply? Because, for example, yesterday when AMD reported, they raised their server CPU business, right, by several billions of dollars. So, that tells me that they have the scale to go and get incremental supply, right?

So, how are you dealing with that question about does Arm have enough scale to go and get the supply to be a meaningful player in the CPU markets, right, given your belief in the technical merits of the product? Thank you.

Rene Haas: Yeah, thank you, Vivek. I'll start, take your second part of your question first, and then Jason will talk about the smartphone scenario that you had described. Your question is a valid one. The way I think about it is that the Arm AGI CPU is our first product. AMD's been at it for a long time. They've got a lot of SKUs. They buy a lot of capacity from TSMC. They have a lot of relationships that they've built over decades. This is our first product. That said, it's not our first relationship with folks like TSMC. It's not our first relationship with memory vendors such as Micron, Samsung, and SK.

They've known us for years and decades, and we've been working pretty diligently to share with them our long-term plans. I think supply for the industry is going to be tight, and as Jason mentioned, we'll talk a bit more about our future outlook in upcoming quarters. But we are going to be working very, very hard to secure the supply that we need for the expanded demand because we think it's very, very, very large. And our partners know that, and we've been talking to them, not for weeks, not for months, but probably a year plus as we've talked about doing this platform. We've looked at this as a long-term endeavor. It's not a one-year single project.

It's a 5-10-year endeavor that's going to require relationships across all the supply chain, and we're very, very serious about making sure we get all that done.

Jason Child: Thanks, Vivek. Regarding the mobile business, when we look at some of the external forecasts, I think IDC has units in mobile growing basically flat. I think it's minus 1% next year. As we talk to partners, I'd say flat is generally what folks are expecting. There's already been kind of the hit and the reduction due to the memory constraints, and I think the expectations are those constraints stay relatively consistent, which basically means flat growth, not further deterioration. And then, because we continue to have more v9 adoption, we're now getting over 50%, so it's a little less of a tail end. But CSS adoption continues to grow.

We also have multiple partners on next generations of CSS, which are at slightly higher royalty rates with and higher chip prices. All that means that we will grow the overall business much faster than the market. Think of it at least being in the kind of double digits plus in growth rate for next year. That's our best guess right now. If we see anything that changes, of course, we'll let you guys know. But that's what industry as well as our partners all seem to think at this point.

Operator: Thank you. We will now take our final question for today. The final question comes from the line of Joe Quatrochi from Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Joe Quatrochi: Yeah, thanks for taking the question. You talked about securing more supply on AGI, and I assume that comes at a higher cost. Can you just kind of talk us through the ability to offset that and how we should think about this, the gross margin puts and takes as you start to ship?

Rene Haas: Yeah, I'm sorry. Could you repeat that one more time?

Joe Quatrochi: Yeah, just I assume that the increased supply that you're getting for AGI is coming at a higher cost. Can you just talk about your ability to offset those higher costs, pass that through to customers in terms of pricing, and then the puts and takes on gross margin?

Rene Haas: Yeah. No, thank you. As I mentioned earlier, the overall cost of the systems, memory being probably the single largest contributor to all that, then you've got kind of downstream other impacts to your point on different parts of the supply chain, definitely put margin pressure. That being said, we do have some elasticity on pricing and the ability to increase it, which I think we've already demonstrated an ability to do that as we've gotten started with the program. I'm actually not as worried on that point relative to offsetting any constraints on supply and cost, and managing it downstream. You've seen public comments from everybody else who's in this business that's what we're doing.

We'll be following where the market goes and making sure that we're not trailing common sense, but at the same time, not trying to cause too much pain on the end customers. It's our first product, we want to make sure everybody wins with it, but I'm not as worried about that piece impacting gross margins.

Jason Child: Yeah, maybe just to reiterate what we said was for this first version, we're expecting to be somewhere in the high 30%s to the low 40% gross margin. For the first version, we expect it to be probably a little lower, then as we develop more expertise, probably rely on doing a little more work ourselves and maybe less from partners over time, which others in the market do. Over time, we'll get ourselves to more of the market standard of 50%+, but I don't expect that to happen on the first version. That's probably going to happen more on the next version.

So, for this version, I would stick to the kind of 30%-40% range, then we'll obviously give you updates on a quarterly basis as we start shipping in Q4.

Operator: Thank you. That was our final question for today. I will now hand the call back to Rene for closing remarks.

Rene Haas: Thank you. Thank you for all the questions. They were very, very timely and excellent questions. Just to summarize, this was a great quarter for the company. 50% licensing growth means a lot of growth coming in the future in royalties, which we feel great about. We also feel very, very good about the fact that our data center business continues to flourish. We had talked for many, many years about Arm getting to 20% in data centers. The fact that we are 50% in the last year and will be 60% by the end of this year is also something we are very, very proud of.

Most importantly, I think what we are now starting to see is what was one great business is now turning into two great businesses. The IP business continues to do very, very well. We are very confident in its growth going forward. But now with our new Arm AGI CPU ramping into production, increased confidence to achieve the $2 billion number that we have been talking about, it just thrills me to be able to talk about two businesses now rather than one that are both going to be on amazing growth paths. Could not be prouder of what the company has achieved, thanking our employees, our partners, and customers who helped make it happen.

So, thank you again for all the questions and comments, and congratulations to the Arm team for a great quarter.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

news.Title: Why It’s Time to Load Up on Arm Stock
news.Content:
Arm Holdings (ARM) stock fell sharply, down 44% over the past month and trading about 63% below its 52-week high. The selloff in ARM stock intensified following the company's second-quarter earnings announcement, as concerns over slowing royalty revenue growth led by the softness in the smartphone market weighed on investor sentiment. Today's broad selloff in chipmakers and AI stocks hasn't done ARM stock any favors either.

Overall, however, Arm's underlying business performance remains encouraging. Strong demand for ARM-based computing architectures helped drive solid growth in both revenue and earnings during the quarter. That said, the smartphone market continues to pose a challenge. Higher memory prices are weighing on smartphone demand, particularly in the mid- and lower-end segments, pressuring royalty revenue. Royalty revenue from edge AI applications was also broadly flat year-over-year (YoY).

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Super Micro Computer Posts Record $19.9 Billion Quarter, But 44% of Revenue Came From a Single Customer

The Oracle Selloff Deepens Despite Strong Long-Term Growth Outlook. How to Play ORCL Stock Here.

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

Management expects these challenges to persist in the near term. While demand from cloud AI and physical AI is expected to support royalty growth, continued weakness in the smartphone market and tough YoY comparisons are likely to limit gains in edge AI. As a result, Arm expects royalty revenue to increase at a low teens rate sequentially but only at a low single-digit rate YoY, pointing to a further slowdown in growth.

Nevertheless, the royalty business is only part of the investment story. Arm continues to see strong demand for its licensing portfolio, which is expected to more than offset the near-term weakness in royalties. Growing adoption of its architecture across AI, cloud computing, and other high-performance computing applications provides solid growth opportunities.

Although the slowdown in royalty revenue and weakness in smartphone demand cannot be overlooked, the recent selloff has created a more attractive risk-reward opportunity.

Arm to Sustain Solid Growth Despite Smartphone Weakness

Arm reported a strong second quarter, and momentum will likely continue. Its revenue rose 27% YoY to $1.44 billion, marking its fifth consecutive quarter of growth above 20%. Growth was largely driven by a 50% increase in licensing revenue to $773 million, reflecting stronger customer demand for Arm's technology and Compute Platform. The higher licensing activity is encouraging, as it indicates that more customers are committing to Arm's architecture, which could translate into higher royalty revenue in the future.

Story Continues

Royalty revenue increased 8% YoY to $670 million, supported by strong demand from cloud AI and physical AI markets. Data center royalties doubled from the previous year as Arm-based CPUs gained traction across AI infrastructure and cloud computing. Physical AI royalties also grew 50%, driven by wider adoption of Arm technology in automotive and robotics.

However, edge AI growth remained relatively flat as higher memory prices continued to weigh on smartphone demand. This weakness was partly offset by higher royalty rates from the growing adoption of Armv9 and its Compute Subsystems (CSS). A recovery in smartphone demand could provide further support to royalty growth over time.

Arm's bottom-line performance was also strong, with adjusted EPS increasing 33% to $0.52, outpacing revenue growth. Another positive development was the improving outlook for Arm's AGI CPU business. Management now sees the opportunity to generate up to $2 billion in revenue across FY2027 and FY2028, compared with its earlier expectation of more than $1 billion. This upbeat guidance follows new purchase orders from multiple customers and supply agreements with supply-chain partners.

Looking ahead to Q3, Arm expects revenue of approximately $1.54 billion, representing around 24% YoY growth, while adjusted EPS is projected at $0.56, up 30%. Licensing revenue is expected to remain strong, with growth above 50%. Royalty growth should continue to benefit from cloud and physical AI demand, although weaker smartphone sales and a challenging comparison base are likely to limit near-term growth.

Overall, Arm's business remains well-positioned to benefit from rising AI-related demand. While weakness in the smartphone market may weigh on near-term royalties, strong licensing activity, growing data center adoption, and contributions from AGI CPUs provide meaningful support for longer-term growth prospects.

ARM Stock's Selloff Is a Buying Opportunity

ARM stock's recent pullback has created an attractive entry point for long-term investors, despite near-term challenges in its royalty business. While persistent weakness in the smartphone market could constrain royalty growth, strong licensing demand, accelerating data center adoption, and the expanding opportunity in AGI CPUs provide multiple growth drivers.

While analysts have a "Moderate Buy" consensus rating on ARM stock, its solid fundamentals and significant share price decline make it an attractive stock to consider now.

news.Title: Is Arm Holdings a Buy After Its Latest Earnings Report?
news.Content:
Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) delivered a record fiscal second quarter, yet its stock has fallen approximately 11.5% as of noon following yesterday's earnings report.

That's an uncomfortable reaction for a company reporting 27% revenue growth, a 33% increase in adjusted earnings and a 50% surge in licensing revenue.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Why is Wall Street selling?

On paper, the AI growth story remains firmly intact. But investors aren't simply buying visible growth anymore. They're demanding evidence that today's AI spending will translate into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

There seems to be an important disconnect between Arm's operating performance and investor expectations. Second-quarter revenue reached $1.44 billion, while data center royalties doubled year-over-year. Management also raised its optimism, now expecting its new AGI CPU — Arm's first production chip to specifically assist agentic AI — to generate up to $2 billion in cumulative revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

But here's where the analysis gets interesting. Licensing and other revenue surged 50% to $773 million, but the Annualized Contract Value (ACV), a better indicator of underlying licensing momentum, grew just 12%. Wall Street seems to be focusing on this divergence.

Large licensing agreements can inflate quarterly revenue, but they don't automatically produce recurring royalties. Customers of Arm's proprietary technology must still design, manufacture, and ship chips before Arm collects those payments.

The metric investors must focus on

It's easy for investors to look at the $773 million in licensing revenue and its 50% growth and assume the business is accelerating.

But Annualized Contract Value (ACV) growth of just 12% is disappointing, and that's the metric investors must keep a close eye on. ACV essentially strips out much of the quarterly noise from large licensing agreements, providing a clearer picture of underlying licensing momentum.

The uncomfortable truth is that while reported licensing growth grew 50%, underlying ACV growth actually slowed.

This doesn't mean Arm's business is deteriorating. It means the headline number looks more attractive than the underlying core driver.

The divergence becomes obvious when we put the last three quarters side by side:

The real investment question isn't whether Arm can book another massive licensing quarter. It's whether those customer commitments become production designs, shipped chips, and recurring royalties.

Arm Holdings signed several large licensing agreements and benefited from the timing and accounting treatment of those deals. The resulting revenue hit the income statement immediately, but the underlying annualized contract base didn't expand nearly as quickly.

Meanwhile, customers continue to invest in Arm technology. More than 60 active ATA subscriptions and additional CSS agreements support the longer-term opportunity. But investors should not mistake upfront licensing revenue for guaranteed future royalties.

Here's the operational reality: Arm licenses technology first. Customers spend months designing chips. Manufacturers then produce those chips. Only when production ramps do recurring royalties follow.

Valuation has little room for error

Arm's business is firing on multiple cylinders, but its valuation leaves very little room for disappointment. Even after the recent 11% sell-off, investors are still paying an extraordinary premium for the company's future growth.

ARM PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts .

As of noon, Arm shares trade at approximately 173 times trailing earnings and more than 75 times forward earnings. That kind of valuation is too large and risky to justify.

Such a premium assumes Arm can successfully convert its licensing momentum into recurring royalties, capture a meaningful share of the AI server CPU market, and scale its AGI CPU business without sacrificing profitability. That's a lot of execution already embedded in the share price.

The risks are not hypothetical. Royalty growth of 8% lagged the explosive licensing performance. AGI CPU shipments have yet to ramp materially; initial gross margins are expected to be just 30–40%, and supply-chain constraints remain an obstacle. Meanwhile, competition from rival chip companies AMD and Intel isn't going away.

Is the stock a buy?

ARM is a compelling long-term business, but at this valuation, I don't see much upside anytime soon. I'd rather remain on the sidelines than chase the AI narrative. Today's decline makes the stock cheaper, but not necessarily cheap in the absolute sense.

I'd rather wait for a more attractive entry point or another quarter confirming that licensing commitments are converting into royalties and AGI shipments.

But, at the end of the day, there's no prize for buying a great company at any price. Arm deserves a place on the watch list, but until valuation catches up with fundamentals, patience may be the better investment strategy.

news.Title: Why Arm Holdings Stock Is Crashing Today
news.Content:
By most measures, the stock should be well up today. The company's record-breaking revenue of $1.44 billion in fiscal Q2 was not only up 27% year over year, but handily topped estimates of $1.38 billion. Earnings improved 33% to $0.52 per share as well, versus a consensus of $0.47. Guidance for the quarter currently underway was healthy too, suggesting top-line growth of 24%.

Nevertheless, as of 12:21 p.m. ET, shares of Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) are down 11.7%, bringing their week-to-date loss to 18%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What gives?

It may be more about the market environment right now than not. But, Arm's second-quarter numbers and third-quarter outlook dished out some degree of disappointment. Taking a cue from other tumbling technology stocks , investors are selling this one too.

Arm Holdings' red flags

Chief among the red flags behind today's sizable sell-off is Arm Holdings' Q2 royalty revenue. While licensing revenue soared 50% to $773 million, royalty revenue only improved by 8% to $670 million, reflecting softness in smartphone memory prices that could linger for the foreseeable future.

This weak royalty number prompted Barclays to lower its price target on ARM from $360 per share to $325, while Goldman Sachs reiterated its sell rating and $160 price target -- compared to the stock's present price near $165 -- on the same concern.

That said, although Arm Holdings' third-quarter revenue guidance of $1.54 billion (+/- $50 million) is technically better than the analyst consensus of $1.53 billion, investors may have been tacitly expecting a stronger growth outlook from the company itself.

Image source: Getty Images.

Perhaps more than anything, however, much of today's selling can be attributed to the sweeping reset most chipmakers' stocks are suffering right now. Shares of Nvidia , Micron , and Qualcomm are also all similarly in the red on Thursday, making it easier for investors to throw in the towel on ARM.

Opportunity knocks (if you can stomach the volatility)

There are real reasons for this sweeping sell-off, to be clear. For instance, Qualcomm's fiscal fourth-quarter handset revenue fell 26%, and guidance for the fiscal first-quarter now underway was lackluster. Other chip companies are seeing similar headwinds.

This correction was inevitable sooner or later, though. It's also the beginning of a buying opportunity, even if we're not necessarily at the exact bottom yet. Just watch out for volatility, which is likely to linger even after the bottom is made and we're on the way back up.

news.Title: Sick of Swings? Same… But History Is on Our Side
news.Content:
The Nasdaq Composite is down more than 4% on Thursday as we write this. Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, especially chipmakers and data center names, are sliding for a second day, both here and in Asia.

Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) has fallen sharply after its smartphone chip sales came in below expectations. Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) is lower despite reporting record revenue, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is adding to Wednesday's 7% drop.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The Nasdaq is still below its record close on Oct. 6. And if you own AI-linked stocks, including many we've recommended, this week alone may have felt like whiplash. Monday brought another drop. On Tuesday night, stock futures fell as election results came in. Wednesday brought relief. This morning, the red is back.

That's a lot to sit through, whether you started with $1,000 in a few stocks or have built a seven-figure portfolio over decades. Either way, the past month has tested our patience.

TMF co-founder and CEO Tom Gardner has never pretended this part is easy. After his October Quarterly Call, he told members he's "happy to give up fractions of future gains for stability." Even he will trade a little return for some peace of mind.

How Fast the Mood Can Turn

Tuesday night showed how quickly things can change. Stock futures fell at first as results came in, then turned higher overnight.

By Wednesday's close, the Dow had jumped 3%. That was its biggest gain the day after a midterm election since 1982, according to CFRA Research.

Picture selling your stocks at 10 p.m. on Tuesday. By Wednesday's close, you'd likely have missed the rally. Today's drop may tempt some of us to make that same mistake.

Co-founder David Gardner has a line for moments like this: "Stocks always go down faster than they go up, but they always go up more than they go down." The drops feel worse because they come so fast. Historically, though, the gains have been bigger.

Owning many stocks makes those drops easier to live through. The Motley Fool now suggests the average member own at least 50, built up over time. With that many businesses across different industries, it's much harder for any single bad morning to sink you.

AI Isn't One Trade

Not every AI stock joined Wednesday's rally. Cloud giants like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) jumped. Chipmakers fell, and so did many companies tied to the data center build-out, such as Vertiv (NYSE:VRT), GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV), and Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE). That happened even as most stocks rose.

Story Continues

If you own a cloud giant, Wednesday may have felt great. If you own a chipmaker, you may have watched your stock slide while nearly everything else climbed. That can feel lonely.

But a few rough days for a stock say little about the business behind it. Big tech companies are still spending heavily on AI, and demand for chips still looks strong. Order books at many data center suppliers also appear to be growing fast, though the ride may stay bumpy. If the companies you own keep growing, short-term swings like this one tend to matter less over time.

"AI stocks" covers very different businesses with different risks, so they won't always move together.

That's why it can help to own a mix of AI businesses, not just one kind. When one part of the trade struggles, another may be holding up.

Two Ways to Stay in the Game

If today's drop has you itching to act, two habits can help. They apply just as well whether you're investing $300 or $30,000.

First, aim to hold for at least three to five years as a minimum. One rough week, or even one disappointing quarter, tells you little about where a business will be by then. When you think in years, an overnight futures move gets much easier to ignore.

Second, keep new bets small. Try a small position in an idea that interests you. If it works out, great. If it doesn't, you've learned something without putting much of your long-term plan at risk.

The Long View

The past month has been uncomfortable, and the swings may not be over yet. We won't pretend otherwise.

But it helps to zoom out. Over the long run, the stock market has historically climbed up and to the right. Since 1874, U.S. stocks have returned about 11% in an average year, counting dividends, according to our research . Past performance does not guarantee future results. Still, that history includes wars, recessions, crashes, and plenty of months like this one.

The Motley Fool's goal is to help you beat the market over time, with a portfolio you don't lose sleep over and actually enjoy owning. That's the goal for us individually, too.
